sections.description: Standalone workshop inventory and production system: raw materials, multi-level recipes, production runs, an auditable movement ledger, a phone PWA, and one-way stock push to a WooCommerce shop via VGC Stock Bridge.
sections.changelog:
1.163.2

The till no longer shows VAT in a company that is not registered for it. The product list handed to the till carried each product’s stored VAT rate, so the cart split a VAT out of every price and the totals panel showed one — in a company that charges none. The till is now told the rate it will actually charge, reads every rate through the same gate as the rest of the app (so a price list it cached offline is right too), and shows neither a Net nor a VAT line when there is no VAT: just the total. Sales already recorded were charged and stored correctly; only the screen was wrong.

A recorded sale’s detail no longer shows a VAT % column reading 0% on every row for such a company.

1.163.1

Fixed: a company that is not VAT registered could not edit a product. The form leaves out the VAT boxes there — a company that charges none has nothing to type in them — but the pricing code still tried to listen to two of them, and that error took the rest of the form’s wiring with it. Both are guarded now, and the form’s wiring is executed by the test suite in both companies, registered and not.

1.163.0

A company that is not VAT registered pays final prices, and now its books say so everywhere. It gets nothing back from the state, so what it pays IS what the goods cost, and every margin is worked out from that figure.

A trade between your companies crosses at the price the buyer actually pays. Selling to the unregistered company, the VAT-inclusive price is what lands in its books — it used to receive the net figure and was short by the VAT on every trade. Asking the registered company for goods, your request is priced as final, so they invoice exactly what you asked for. A non-registered company selling to a registered one is unchanged: there was never any VAT in that price to claim.

Purchases already booked the old way are restated once, on the first page load after the update: the mirrored purchase keeps its number and its received quantities, and only the cost changes. Margins in the unregistered company will drop by the VAT — that money was never yours to keep.

The screens now agree with the server. A VAT-inclusive document in an unregistered company used to show a cost about 17% below what was stored, and a margin that much too flattering: on the purchase page, the order page and the printed order sheet.

1.162.0

A trade can start from either company. A purchase whose vendor is one of your own companies now goes over to that company as an order request — you ask for what you need, it appears on their orders list, and nothing is typed twice. Their sales order to you still arrives here as a purchase, as before.

They accept or decline. Until a request is accepted it counts for nothing there: no goods leave, no turnover, nothing owed. Accepting turns it into an ordinary order and your purchase becomes its mirror, so from then on their order leads and what they send is what you receive. Declining leaves your purchase marked Declined, for you to change and ask again — or delete.

Your figures, theirs to adjust. The request carries your quantities and prices; they may change the prices before accepting, and every save of yours rewrites it until they do. A product they have not got stops the request and is named — tick it into that company on the product and save again.

1.161.0

A maker’s goods sold at the till count on their consignment purchase. Selling goods a maker left on consignment now raises that purchase’s Sold and lowers its Still held, and the maker is owed on the purchase at the price it agreed — no separate note. The oldest delivery goes first; a refund gives the units back to the delivery they came from. Goods taken in on a Take on consignment note still go on a note.

Sold can go up, never below what the till sold. Typing a lower figure, dropping the line, switching the purchase to bought, or deleting it is refused while receipts are booked on it — refund the receipt instead. This is what stops a maker being billed twice.

Received at. A consignment purchase says where the goods were left: the workshop, or a store. Goods left at a store are that store’s to sell, without walking them over.

The main counter. Only the till marked Primary sells from the workshop’s stock. A site with a single till now has it marked on its own; with several and none marked, the Locations screen and the till say so, and the till opens on the main counter when there is one.

1.160.0

A product in more than one company. On a product, Also in (administrators, when there is more than one company) ticks the companies that should have it too, the way Visible to does for a partner. The other company gets the product under the same SKU — a product you make arrives there as a bought-in product supplied by you — and its name, unit, VAT rate, category, photo, barcode, pack, shelf life and notes are kept the same both ways, whichever side you edit. Stock, prices, costs, recipes and the shop stay each company’s own. Untick, and the other company keeps it as an ordinary product of its own. The product page says where else it is, with a link, and the lists tag it Shared.

1.159.0

The whole palette follows the accent. Choosing a company’s colour under Settings → Look now recolours everything that carried the default’s warmth — page and card backgrounds, lines, text shades, the dark panel, shadows — not only the buttons and links. Each keeps its lightness; only the hue moves to yours, and a greyish accent fades the tint down to neutral grey. The first swatch is the app’s own hand-drawn palette, exactly as before.

1.158.0

Move an order to another company. On an order that nothing has happened to yet — nothing sent, nothing paid — a manager in both companies finds Move to <company> among the actions. The order arrives there under a new number of its own, its items matched by SKU (an item the other company lacks stops the move and is named), the customer becomes visible there if not already, and the customer’s total stays what it was even across the VAT boundary. The source keeps the order as a frozen record marked Moved, under its old number, counting for nothing and linking to where it went; moving it back revives that record, and deleting the moved order removes it. Anything already sent, paid or completed is refused with the reason.

1.157.0

An accent colour per company. Settings → Look picks the colour the app is painted in — buttons, links, the active tab, the till — from a row of swatches or any colour you like, and the whole app previews it as you choose; nothing changes until you save. Each company keeps its own, so which company you are in shows at a glance, and the Companies list shows each one’s dot. Leave it unset and the app stays exactly as it was.

1.156.1

Fix: the Settings screen crashed (“boot is not defined”) when the shop pull was on and the shop listed its payment gateways. The fee-rules card, added in 1.151.0, reached for a value a template does not have; it only ran once the pull was switched on and gateways were listed, which is why it surfaced now. The screen renders again; the fee rules take their currency from the settings themselves.

1.156.0

A refund in the shop reaches the books. Units the shop refunded on an order come back here on the next pull: the sale is refunded line by line, the money comes off, and for an online sale the goods walk home to the workshop shelf — exactly as a refund rung at the till would. Money the shop gave back beyond its lines (postage, a goodwill amount) has no goods behind it, so it is noted on the sale and moves nothing. Check against the shop reports refunds too.

Update Stock Bridge to 0.7.0 on the shop: it sends what was refunded per line, and it returns the orders whose refunds changed even when the shop did not mark the order itself as modified.

1.155.0

Trade between your companies. Raise an order in one company to the other (it is in the partner list as Your company) and the other company receives it as a purchase of its own the moment you save — numbered after the order, from a vendor that is you. What you mark as sent is what arrives there: the order takes the goods off your shelf and the mirrored purchase puts them on theirs, in one save. The price on the order is the cost on the purchase; whether you charge VAT follows your company’s VAT status. A product the other company has never had is created there by SKU, with you as its supplier and its category made to match.

One author. The mirrored purchase is read-only on the other side — no Save, Complete or Delete there — and its payments are the order’s payments. Change quantities, prices, dates, payments, completion or delete the order, and the purchase follows. Each half links to the other for anyone who may work in both companies.

An order to one of your companies is always Pay in full; a stock note cannot be raised to your own company; display pieces on such an order stay on loan and are not mirrored. If the other company could not receive the mirror, the order says so and saving it again repeats the attempt.

1.154.1

More than one company in the app. Settings → Companies (administrators) creates a second company with its own books — its own stock, sales, purchases, production, business costs, settings, letterhead and shop link. A selector under the app’s name in the sidebar (and in the phone menu) switches between the companies you may work in; the one you chose last is where you land next time. A new company starts with this company’s general settings but no shop link: a shop belongs to one company, and the app refuses to link the same shop twice.

Access is a level per company. Settings → Team shows one company at a time; the level someone had before is their level in the first company, and in any other they have nothing until you give them one.

Partners are shared on demand. One partner list; a partner is seen by the company that made it and by any other an administrator ticks under Visible to on its form, with its own prices, orders and balance in each. Once there are two companies, each appears in the other’s partner list as Your company — the counterparty for trade between them, coming next.

A till installed before there were companies keeps working as it is; a till for another company’s location is installed from that company and is its own app on the phone. Work saved offline replays into the company it was made in, whichever company the screen shows by then.

Fix: a fresh install (and a new company) lost its expense categories on its first load. The one-time category-scope migration rewrote the six expense categories seeded moments earlier as product categories, so the Business costs screen started with an empty category list. Found by the new company on staging; it had been so for every fresh install since 1.135.0. Existing installs are unaffected.

1.153.0

Groundwork for keeping more than one company in the app. Nothing changes on screen. Every table and every setting is now reached through a seam that knows which company a request is about, so a second company (next release) gets its own books — its own stock, sales, purchases, settings and shop link — while the partner list is shared between them. This install is company 1: every table and setting keeps its name, and no data moves.

Access is now a level per company: the level you have today is your level in company 1. Another company grants nothing until you are given a level there.

The daily housekeeping and the hourly pull from the shop run once per company. The uninstaller now also removes the sale_held_notes table, which it had missed.

1.152.0

Check against the shop. A new button in Settings → Orders from the shop compares every order since the start date with the sale in the books and lists, order by order, what differs: missing here, different, or no longer counted as sold. Nothing changes until you press Apply. Applying brings in what is missing, reverses what the shop cancelled, and rewrites any sale that disagrees with the shop — which is how orders imported before the 1.151.0 discount fix get corrected.

A correction to 1.151.0’s notes: they said re-pulling would fix orders imported before the discount fix. It does not — the hourly pull only looks at orders the shop has changed. Check against the shop is the way.

Past orders for the books only. Orders placed before a date you choose are brought in for their money — they appear in sales, profit and reports — but their goods are not taken off the shelf again, because they left long ago. That date is set to the day you switched the pull on, so bringing in history can never count the same goods twice. Past sales are costed at today’s product cost, so profit for those months is approximate.

A card fee estimated from your rule is now replaced by the real one when the gateway reports it later.

Update Stock Bridge to 0.6.1 on the shop: it fixes a fault where a single refund could stop every later order from coming in.

1.151.0

Fix: a discount the shop recorded as a negative line was being thrown away, so an imported order read higher than the customer actually paid — 66.00 where the shop had charged 61.20. Most discount and loyalty plugins apply their discount exactly that way. Re-pull the affected orders and they correct themselves.

What it costs to take the money is now recorded. Where the payment gateway reports the fee it deducted — Stripe and PayPal both do — that exact figure is used. For gateways that report nothing, set a percentage and a fixed amount per payment method in Settings → Orders from the shop. Leave a row blank and nothing is estimated for it.

Each fee lands as a business cost against its own order, dated the order, in a Card fees category kept out of what a product costs to make — taking a card payment is a cost of selling, not of making. Cancel the order and the fee goes with it.

Shipping was checked against the shop line by line in every shape it comes in: flat, free, two carriers on one order, amounts that do not divide, with VAT and without, with prices entered inclusive of tax and with tax rounded at the subtotal. It matches to the stotinka in all of them.

Needs Stock Bridge 0.6.0 on the shop for the card fees.

1.150.0

The shop’s orders come into the books. Switch it on in Settings → Orders from the shop, tick which of the shop’s own statuses mean the goods have gone, and every hour the app reads what the website has sold. Each order becomes a sale at a location called Online shop — so turnover, profit, margin, the chart, the CSV and every report already include the website, with nothing else to set up.

Stock moves the way it does at the counter. An online sale takes its goods off the workshop shelf as it is recorded, so what you have on hand stays true.

A cancelled or refunded order reverses itself. When the shop moves an order out of those statuses the sale is voided and the goods come back — nothing is deleted, the receipt stays with the reason on it.

Postage and fees are counted, as their own lines, so the app’s total is exactly what the customer paid. A product the shop sold that the workshop has never heard of is imported too, as money, and flagged so you can pull that product in and have it match next time.

Needs Stock Bridge 0.5.1 on the shop. Nothing is ever written to the shop: orders are read only, and no name, address, email or phone is transferred.

1.149.0

Say whether the shop’s stock is yours to write. A new switch in Settings → Shop connection. Left on, nothing changes: the shop mirrors the workshop, making stock raises its level, and Set shop = local is there as before.

Switched off, the number in the shop is treated as what it really is for many workshops — an order allowance you set there to cap how many orders come in — and nothing in the app ever writes it again. Not a production run, not a stock note, an order or a purchase, and not the Shop screen, whose overwrite button disappears rather than being left to fail. Auto-push goes dead instead of quietly doing nothing.

The Shop screen becomes Shop allowance: the same levels, read from the shop, so you can see how much of each allowance is left.

1.148.0

A location’s list can be settled out of stock you already have. Until now the only way to clear what a stall or a counter was owed was to log a production run — so if you had already made the batch, the app made it again: materials used up for candles sitting in a box, and the workshop’s count left that much too high. A row whose product is on the workshop shelf now offers Send from stock first. It walks the units over and makes nothing.

It tells you what it will do. The row says how many are at the workshop and the button says how many would go. If the shelf has three and the list wants five, three go over and two stay on the list for whoever goes to the bench — nothing is produced behind your back.

Log production is still one tap away, for the evening you really did make extra and nobody wrote it down. Products you buy in are unchanged: their way out is still the delivery.

1.147.1

Fix: a partner’s logo would not save. You could pick one, you could see it in the picker, and the moment you saved it was gone. The screen was sending it and the database was ready for it — the step in between kept a list of the fields it accepts, and the logo had never been added to it, so it was dropped without a word of complaint.

Your own logo was never affected. Partners you already tried to give a logo to simply need it picking again.

1.147.0

Your logo, and your partners’. Settings → Printed documents gains a logo. It is printed on every document you hand somebody — the order sheet, the goods-received note, the till receipt — and shown in the app’s own sidebar, on the sign-in screen and at the top of the till.

Each partner can have one too. Their page and the partners list show it in place of the coloured initial, it appears beside their name on documents to and from them, and on an item you buy from them it sits beside the supplier’s name.

Any shape. A wide wordmark and a square roundel are both fitted into the space without cropping or stretching, so there is no size to get right before uploading. A workshop with no logo looks exactly as it did before.

1.146.0

Print what arrived. A saved delivery gains a goods-received note on your own headed paper: the document number, who the goods came from, when they arrived, and every line that actually turned up — with the quantity, the agreed price for one and what the line is worth.

On a consignment delivery it says so, totals as value if all sold, and states that the goods remain the supplier’s until sold or bought. On an outright buy it says bought outright and values the goods without pretending to be a bill. A short delivery shows what was ordered beside what came; one that arrived in full does not repeat itself.

Two ruled lines at the foot, delivered by and received by, so whoever brought them can keep a signed copy.

1.145.0

A maker’s goods can be at a market stall. Until now they were simply “held”; now they are held somewhere. A sale location’s page gains A maker’s goods: what is here, what is still at the workshop, and a button to send them over or back. The quantity defaults to all of them.

A till sells the maker’s goods that are at it. The workshop counter sells the workshop’s, a stall sells what has been carried to it — the same rule your own stock follows. A stall will no longer sell a candle that is sitting in the workshop.

A refund puts them back where they were sold from. Moving goods never changes what you owe: the maker holds the same number, in a different place.

1.144.0

The till can see a maker’s goods, and sells them properly. Stock taken on consignment is really on your counter and really for sale — it is simply not yours. The till counts it, shows the split on the tile (“4 + 6 held”) and says on the cart line how many of that line are a maker’s.

Selling one books what you owe. The moment the sale is charged, a Sold from held note is raised against the maker, oldest consignment first: their held stock goes down and what you owe them goes up. No paperwork to remember at the end of a market day. Your own stock always goes first.

A refund gives them back to the maker, not onto your shelf — a part refund cancels the note and re-issues a smaller one, so the trail reads as what really happened. Voiding or deleting the receipt does the same. The receipt’s profit is honest too: a maker’s unit cost you what you owe them.

A till away from the workshop now refuses to sell more than is really there — yours plus the makers’ — and says which is which.

1.143.0

Things on a delivery that are not stock. A purchase now has two tabs — Materials and Other purchases. Put the machine, the pallet charge or the training day on the second one: it needs a name, an amount and, if you like, a cost category.

The cost goes straight to Business costs, dated the delivery and named after the document it came from. Change the line and the cost follows; take the line off, or delete the delivery, and the cost goes with it.

It counts as money you owe the vendor — in the VAT, in the balance, in what you have paid — but never as goods: it has no selling price and no units, so it cannot flatter the profit on a delivery. The delivery’s discount is shared over it too. A new Equipment category ships with it, deliberately kept out of the per-product overhead share.

1.142.0

Vendor discounts on a delivery. A discount can sit on one line, on the whole delivery, or both — as a percentage or as an amount off. Press Show discounts on a purchase to open a strip under each line; the discount for the whole delivery is in the terms card at the top.

A delivery discount is spread over the lines by value, so every material’s cost per unit falls by its own share and what a candle costs you stays true. It comes off before VAT, so the VAT and what you owe the vendor fall with it, the way the invoice reads.

A discount bigger than the line is cut down to fit and says so, so a line can never go below zero. The suggested selling price does not move: a discount you negotiated is extra profit, not a cheaper shelf.

1.141.0

Material audit — a page of its own under Stock for counting materials: weigh or count what is in the workshop, type it in each material’s unit, save, and see which materials do not match the books. Each gap stays open until you tick what explains it — usually a production run or use nobody logged — or write the rest off.

Stock count is now for products, at the workshop or a sale location. Each page lists only its own gaps; the Overview still shows them all.

1.140.0

Stock count. Count what is really on the shelf — at the workshop or a sale location — and see the difference from the books. Made 30, counted 10: 20 missing, and it stays on a list until it is explained. Nothing is changed for you.

Count one item with the new Count button on any product or material, or a whole shelf from Stock → Stock count.

Closing the gap: record what really happened where you always would — the forgotten sales at the till, the production run, the delivery — then tick it on the gap and press These explain it. A new sale after the count can be left unticked. What nothing explains can be written off against the count; if a ticked sale is refunded or a run undone, the gap reopens.

1.139.0

Product names in an order's lines link to the product, display pieces included. As everywhere, a name looks like plain text until you point at it.

Leaving an order never loses an edit. Follow a name while the order has unsaved changes and it is saved first, and you are told so. If the save fails, you stay with your changes. A new order left this way is created, and Back returns to it.

Ctrl-click (Cmd on a Mac, or Shift) opens a product in a new tab and leaves the page you are on untouched, on every product link.

1.138.0

Product names no longer look any different at rest. The underline from 1.137.0 is gone. A name reads as plain text; point at it and it turns orange with a hand cursor, and a tap opens the product.

The closing count links its product names too. If you follow one while the count is not saved, the count is saved first and you are told so. If the save fails, you stay, with your numbers still in the boxes.

The services a sale location offers now show their names like everything else, instead of as an orange block.

1.137.0

Product names are links to the product, all over the app — sale locations, reports, overheads, labour, consignment, partners and shop stock. Tap a name and you land on its page.

And they look like links. About ten names already were, and nothing showed it: the app styled every link as plain text. Product names now carry a quiet underline that brightens on hover.

Where a name deliberately does not link: the till (a tap there sells), search pickers (a tap there selects), and any line you are still editing, because leaving the screen would lose what you have typed.

1.136.0

Picking a standard cost in a recipe is now something you can find. The picker has been on every cost line since 1.134.0, but the only way to reach it was to add a line first and then notice a dropdown reading “One-off” — so it read as though the feature was not there at all.

The Other costs card now offers the choice where the choice is made: Add a standard cost and Add a one-off cost, side by side. The first lands on a real standard cost, already priced, with the picker beside it to change which. A workshop that has not set any up yet gets the one-off button and a link to where standard costs are made.

1.135.0

What the business spends, and what it adds to a product. Power, water, rent, advertising and sundries were recorded nowhere — so every product cost in the app understated what the thing really costs to put on a shelf.

A new Business costs screen records them: what for, category, supplier, date, and the amount with or without VAT. Describe the rent once and each month the screen tells you which bills have not been entered yet, and offers to enter them with the usual amount, ready to correct. Nothing is ever entered for you — a bill you have not paid is not a cost.

A new Overheads tab in Reports divides what was spent by what was made and shows one figure added to every unit, beside what each product cost to make, what it costs with overheads, and the margin that leaves. It changes nothing: the figure is in no product’s cost, no margin and no sale.

And it refuses to double-count. Mark a category such as wages as already inside product cost and it stays in the spend total but out of the per-unit figure; event costs stay in their own event’s profit; and with nothing produced you get a dash rather than “0.00 a unit”, which would read as overheads costing nothing.

1.134.0

Standard costs — amortisation, power, water — named once and priced once. Until now every recipe carried its own typed-in figure for these, so nobody could say what mould wear had cost across the workshop, and putting the price up meant reopening every recipe.

A new Standard costs page holds them: a name, what one of it is — a candle, a batch, an hour — and what one costs. A recipe line then picks one and says how much of it that recipe uses, and the money follows the rate, exactly as a labour line follows the hourly rate.

Changing a rate shows you what it would do first: which products move, from what to what, per finished item. What has already been made keeps the cost it was booked at. A type recipes use cannot be deleted — it can be retired, which stops it being offered for new lines and leaves every existing recipe exactly as it is.

Nothing is migrated and no figure moves: every cost line you have today stays a typed-in one-off until you choose a type for it.

1.133.0

The product page now says which cost it is showing. A candle whose recipe screen said 2.55 while its product page said 3.92 was not a bug: the page shows what the thing really cost the last time it was made, and the recipe shows what it should cost today. Both are right — and nothing said so.

Under the figure there is now one line naming its origin — from what it last cost to make — and when today’s recipe disagrees, recipe today € 2.55 beside it. Every other origin names itself too.

The Bulgarian label on the recipe panel read the same words as the product page, so two different figures looked like one contradicting itself; it now reads “по рецепта”. No figure anywhere in the app changed.

1.132.0

A leftover with no price is no longer sold at nothing. On the closing count, a product nobody has priced now says no price where the money goes. It used to show “0.00”, which looks exactly like a real price — and settling turned it into a genuine sale at zero: the stock gone, no takings, and the event’s profit reading as though you had given them away.

Type the price on the row. Where one is missing the row now offers a box for it, and the money beside it follows as you type. Settling refuses while anything left over has no price, and names the product.

A price you deliberately set to nothing is still a price and settles as before. Bringing an unpriced product all the way home needs no price at all — only what is sold needs one.

1.131.0

A custom piece that has sold leaves the product list and the till. It was made once, to order, and will not be made again — so it stops cluttering the two places you pick from every day.

A new Custom products page holds them all, sold or not: what each one was, when it was made and how many, where any of it still is, and what it cost against what it was priced at.

“Sold” means nothing left anywhere — the workshop plus every location. A piece on a market stall’s table is not sold and stays sellable there, and anything that comes back is simply on the list again. An ordinary product that has run out is untouched: it will be made again, and stays where it was.

1.130.0

Finished products in a custom order. The picker on the custom-order screen now lists finished products as well as materials — two candles going into a gift box, say. Materials still come first under their own heading; finished products sit under a second one, each tagged Product, and search narrows both at once.

A product comes off its own shelf. Using two finished candles takes two candles off the candle shelf — not the wax and wicks they were made from, which left when the candles were made. The commission is costed at what each candle cost to make.

Not enough on the shelf is said before you save, exactly as for a material. Also fixed on the same card: on a phone, each row's spoiled box ran off the edge of the screen.

1.129.0

Put a product straight onto the closing count. For a festival that is already over and a list on paper: no production run per product, no push per product. Search, say how many were there, and it is on the count.

Two boxes per row — Were there and Came home — because that is what the paper says. One pass down the list is enough, and what came home is parked rather than settled, so nothing becomes a fact until you press Settle the count.

The whole list goes in as one write. If any row is refused the lot is rolled back and the message names the row — a list half entered is worse than one refused.

An event may record more than the workshop has, because that is what happened. The workshop honestly goes negative, the debt card says what still needs making, and company inventory never changes by a penny.

1.128.0

Save progress on a closing count. Thirty rows is an hour of unpacking, interrupted. The count can now be put down and picked up — the figures are parked, and the sheet comes back with them already in the boxes.

A parked count changes nothing: no stock moves, no sale is rung up, nothing is written off. Settle the count is still the only button that makes any of it true, and the sheet says so in as many words — so a screen full of restored numbers is never mistaken for a weekend already dealt with.

A sheet the server turns down no longer costs you the rest of the count. Rows whose stock moved while the count was parked are flagged, with what the books said at the time.

1.127.0

Given away. The closing count gains a third box beside Came home and Missing. Samples to the organiser, one to the stall next door, a raffle prize — they come off the shelf at what they cost you and earn nothing.

Without it, anything handed out fell into the leftover and was invoiced as a sale at full price, inventing takings nobody ever received.

A gift and a loss are kept apart, on the ledger and in the P&L: six candles handed to the organiser is a decision, six that vanished is a problem. The P&L gains its own Given away line, at cost, and both come off the profit.

1.126.0

Type the figure on the invoice. The event-cost form gains a With VAT box beside the net one. Fill either and the other works itself out — 144 with VAT at 20% is 120 net, and 100 with VAT is 83.3333. No more reaching for a calculator first.

Changing the rate re-derives from whichever side you typed, so it never rewrites the number you just copied off the receipt. Net is still what gets stored and what the P&L reads — the same rule the consignment note lines have followed since 1.9.0. A company that charges no VAT sees neither box, just the one amount.

19 new checks and eleven reinstated faults confirmed to fail them. The two-way fill is executed against a real form rather than read out of the source — the first version of that guard matched the same line in a different handler and stayed green with the binding deleted.

1.125.0

VAT on what an event cost. The cost form gains a rate box, starting on 20% like a purchase line does. 1.124.0 stored the VAT but never asked for it, so every hotel bill went in VAT-free — fixed.

The card now says what there is to reclaim, in green beside what was spent: 220.00 spent · 36.00 VAT to reclaim. Shown beside the spend and never added to it — VAT you get back is not what the weekend cost you.

A company that is not VAT registered gets no rate box at all, rather than one sitting at nought asking to be filled in. The P&L is unchanged and still entirely net of VAT, which is the right basis when you reclaim it. 10 new checks, seven reinstated faults confirmed to fail them.

1.124.0

What it cost to be there. Every event gets a costs card: the hotel, the diesel, the pitch fee, the market tax. Recorded net with the VAT beside it, so a company that charges none sees one figure rather than two that agree.

These belong to the event and to nothing else. They never reach an item’s cost, an average or a recipe. Spreading a hotel bill over the candles is a tempting idea that would quietly change the margin on every product sold anywhere, for ever — so it does not happen, and a test proves it.

And whether it paid. A statement that reads down the page: takings, what the goods cost, gross profit and margin, what never came back, what it cost to be there — ending in one number. A weekend that lost money says so in red.

The takings are scoped to the event, not to its dates. The settlement sale is written when the van is unpacked, which is after the event ended; a date window would have left a whole weekend’s unrecorded takings out of its own P&L. Every figure is net of VAT — VAT was never ours. What never came back is valued at what it costs to make today, which is an estimate and says so. Manager-only throughout.

77 new checks, twenty-four reinstated faults confirmed to fail them, and 38 more run on staging against the real sales report — including a direct check that the P&L and the sales screen agree about the same weekend. A new guard also catches something that nearly shipped here: two functions of the same name in one file, where the second silently replaces the first.

1.123.0

The closing count. Unpack the van and say what came home. Every product that was ever at the event gets a row: what went, what was rung up, what the books say should be left — and two boxes for you, came home and missing.

What is left over was sold. Ten went, four were rung up, two came home and one is missing: the other three were sold and nobody wrote it down. The app records them as an ordinary sale at the event, so they reach takings, VAT and profit like any other. That is how a weekend where nobody touched the till still gets its takings in.

What came home goes back to the workshop. What did not is written off — off the event and nowhere else, because a candle that was dropped is genuinely gone. The write-off is costed, so it can be seen for what it is.

The count either settles or it does not. A row that counts back more than the books ever had stops the whole sheet before a single line is written — a half-settled event, stock home with the takings never recorded, is the worst thing that could come out of this. Boxes start on what the books say, so an untouched sheet sells nothing and loses nothing. Manager-only, because it writes revenue.

66 new checks, twenty reinstated faults confirmed to fail them, and 32 more run on staging — where the resulting sale, its VAT and its frozen cost were read back off the real tables. Next: event costs and the P&L they feed.

1.122.0

Events: a sale location that exists for a weekend. Pick Event as the kind and give it the dates it runs. It shows in the list with where it has got to — Upcoming, Running now, To settle, Settled — worked out from the dates, so it keeps up on its own.

Load the van with what you have not made yet. Pushing to an event is no longer capped at what the workshop holds: take ten candles with seven in stock and all ten go, with the workshop showing minus three. That is the truth of it — three left the building that were never logged as made — and what the company owns is unchanged. Every other location still refuses, and an event refuses too unless the quantity is deliberately set above what is there.

The row says so before you press the button, and the shortfall is listed on the event afterwards under Taken but never made. One tap logs the production run (or the delivery) that squares it. Nothing is sent anywhere — the goods are already at the event, which is what makes this different from the make-and-send list.

Closing an event freezes its figures. No more sales or pushes until it is reopened. It will not close while anything is outstanding, and says exactly what: units still there to pull back, units the workshop has not made, entries on the make-and-send list.

104 new checks, twenty-nine reinstated faults confirmed to fail them, and 40 more run on staging through the real routes — where one real fault was caught before release: the form sent the event dates and the create route quietly dropped them. Next: event costs and a per-event P&L.

1.121.0

Plan what to make and take to a location, before anything is sold. Every sale location now has a To make and send list with an Add button: pick a product, say how many, and it goes on the list. Nothing moves — no stock leaves the workshop, the location’s count does not budge — until you settle it.

It is the same list the till fills by selling short, read forwards instead of backwards. One button still settles either kind: it logs the production run (or the delivery) the job needs and delivers those units to that location. A row that mixes the two says so — 5 sold, not logged + 3 planned — because they are the same trip to the bench.

Only a plan can be taken back off. Changing your mind about something you meant to make is ordinary. An entry caused by a real sale is the explanation for a real negative on a real shelf, and erasing it would turn a job somebody can do into a mystery nobody can — so the app will not.

A plan never hides a problem. The Count is off flag on a location is still suppressed only by something genuinely sold-and-unlogged; a plan explains no discrepancy, so it suppresses nothing. The card only wears the alarm colour when something really was sold ahead of the books, and settling a plan is recorded as Made for … rather than Logged after selling at ….

89 new checks, twenty-one reinstated faults confirmed to fail them, and 32 more run on staging through the real routes against the real database. No schema change.

1.120.0

Selling ahead of the books now works at every location, not only the workshop counter — but you have to say so. Go past what a stall has on its shelf and the line grows a Sell as backlog tick; nothing is charged until it is answered, and then it goes on that location’s Sold but not logged yet list exactly as it does at the counter.

Nothing is walked over from the workshop. At the workshop counter the app moves stock across as it sells, because the bench is behind you. A market stall is somewhere else entirely, so stock still gets there the way it always did — you push it. Settling the list afterwards logs the production run (or the delivery) and delivers those units to that stall, which puts its count straight.

The stall’s wall still shows what is on the table. Products that were never pushed there stay out of sight until you search for one by name, and then they appear under a divider that says Not at this location. They are not greyed out — selling one is the whole point — and they say “not here” rather than a bare nought.

Refusing by default is deliberate. At the workshop counter a shortfall nearly always means “made and not written down”. At a stall it usually means somebody miscounted, so the app keeps saying no until you tell it otherwise. Lowering the quantity back to what is on the shelf clears the tick again. The charge button says what would open it rather than sitting there dead, and on a phone the dock says a line is waiting for an answer.

73 new checks, twenty reinstated faults confirmed to fail them, and 29 more run on staging against the real database — where one real fault was caught before release: two lines of the same product, ticked once, recorded only half of what was owed. No schema change.

1.119.0

Recipe templates. Keep the set of lines you always start with, then stamp it onto a new product instead of typing it out again. Every recipe now has Start from a template and Save as template — and saving one you already built is how the first templates get made, because you have the recipes already and retyping one to seed the rest is exactly the chore this removes.

A line can be left open. Instead of naming an item, call it “The fragrance”; applying the template then asks you to pick one before it will write anything. That is what lets a single template cover a dozen recipes that differ only by a scent, rather than keeping a dozen near-copies of the same thing.

Change the batch size and the amounts follow. A template written for ten candles applied to twenty doubles the wax and still uses one wick each — per-run amounts scale, per-item amounts do not. Type over any of them and your number wins. Labour and other costs come across as well, not only materials.

Applying adds to what is there. A component already on the recipe is skipped rather than duplicated, and anything you added by hand is left alone. Replacing the whole recipe is available, but you have to ask for it. What the preview shows is worked out by the same code that does the writing, so the panel cannot promise one thing and do another.

A template is a rubber stamp, not a link. Once applied it is an ordinary recipe owned by the product: editing the template afterwards changes nothing already made from it, and deleting one is always safe because nothing depends on it. The flip side is worth knowing — fixing a template fixes the recipes you make after the fix, not the ones already made.

61 new checks, twelve reinstated faults confirmed to fail them — among them scaling that doubled the wick, an applied template that threw away the recipe it was added to, and a template edit that reached back into recipes already made — and the whole path run again on staging against the real database.

1.118.1

Fixed: the till squashed every product card when the list got long. With a full catalogue on the primary counter the wall tried to fit all of it on one screen instead of scrolling — at around 240 products each card was seven pixels tall, a stripe of colour with nothing readable on it.

Cards are now always the same size, whatever the catalogue holds, and the wall scrolls. They are also the same size as each other: a short name or a long price no longer makes one card taller than the one beside it. Measured in a real browser at four screen widths and four catalogue sizes, from eight products up to 240.

Only visible since 1.118.0, when the primary counter started listing everything for sale rather than the handful of items pushed to a stall.

1.118.0

One sale location can now be the primary one — the workshop’s own counter. Mark it on the location page and every product you sell is on its till straight away, whether or not it has been pushed there. No more running to the app to push a box of candles before you can ring one up.

Stock is taken from the workshop as it sells, not in advance — behind the scenes that writes exactly the transfer you would have written by hand, so the workshop count drops when the goods actually leave and what the company owns still adds up. Anything already pushed to that counter is used first.

Selling something you have not logged yet no longer stops you. At the primary counter it goes through, because it means you made it and had not got round to writing it down. Every other location still refuses — a market stall with nothing on the table is a genuine shortage, not a paperwork lag.

What you owe the books is written down for you. The location page gets a Sold but not logged yet list: how many, of what, and one button. Tapping it logs the production run (or the delivery, for something you buy in) that really happened, moves the units to the counter, and puts the count straight. Entries are grouped by product, because one trip to the bench settles them all.

Refunding or voiding a sale takes its job back off that list. And a shortfall the list already explains is no longer also flagged as an unexplained count problem: To log when there is a known cure, Count is off when there is not.

1.117.0

Fixed: a lot price no longer loses money to rounding. Entering 82.42 for 1000 g showed a cost of 82.40. The app was working out the price per unit, rounding it, and multiplying it back up — and that error grows with the quantity, so the bigger the delivery the further the document drifted from the invoice it exists to mirror. A lot-priced line now totals the figure you typed, exactly, and the VAT and what you owe follow from that.

Both prices are now always on screen, and you can fill in either one. Per unit and Lot price sit side by side on every line: type whichever the invoice gives you and the other fills itself in. The one that was worked out is shown recessive, with a dashed outline, so the row always says which figure is doing the work — and it stays editable, because typing in it is exactly how you switch which one counts. The old per-unit/per-lot toggle is gone.

A derived unit price is now shown and stored to six decimal places instead of four: 82.42 over 1000 g is 0.08242 a gram, and 0.0824 is a figure that does not multiply back to the invoice.

Purchase lines are a wider row than they were, so the point where each line becomes a stacked card moved from 1100px to 1240px. Nothing is hidden at any width.

1.116.0

Best-before dates on purchases. Every line of a delivery now has its own Best before box. Until now the only place to date a delivery was Receive stock on an item page, so anything arriving on a purchase document — which is how most stock arrives — could not be dated at all.

The date follows the goods: receiving the delivery puts it on the stock entry, which is what the Goes off list on the item page reads. Correcting a date after the goods have arrived updates that entry too, so a typo is a fix rather than something to undo and redo.

Products can say how long they keep. A new Shelf life on the product — "18 months", "14 days" — and every delivery of it then arrives with the best-before already worked out, on purchase lines and hand-entered deliveries alike. You can still change it for a particular batch: the shelf life is what the product keeps for in general, and a jar can always say otherwise.

A month means a calendar month: 18 months from 15 January is 15 July. Counting a month as 30 days would have dated a real jar a week early.

Leave the shelf life empty and nothing changes — no dates are invented and the box on a purchase line simply stays blank. Most of a candle workshop does not go off.

1.115.0

Offline work can no longer be done twice, or thrown away. Two faults in the queue that keeps the app usable at a market stall with no signal.

If a saved change reached the server but the reply got lost coming back, the app assumed it had failed and sent it again — so a delivery could be received twice, or a production run could consume every material a second time and yield candles nobody made. Every stock entry and every production run now carries an id from the moment you tap Save, and the server refuses the same id twice.

If the server refused a queued change when it caught up — not enough stock left, the item was archived — that change was silently deleted. An afternoon at a stall could disappear with nothing said. Refused work is now kept and shown on the Overview under Not synced, with the server’s own reason, to fix and retry or discard deliberately.

A location whose books do not add up now says so. A sale location’s count was floored at zero, so a stall that had sold more than it was recorded receiving read as an ordinary empty shelf. The real figure is kept, the location is flagged Count is off, and the location page names which items and by how much.

A note marked paid by mistake can be put back. Settling was a one-way tap that wrote off a real debt for good. Managers now get Not paid after all.

Undoing a push to a location now records which one it undid — with three pushes of the same item, cancelling the first was logged against the third.

Also fixed: a database-upgrade error introduced in 1.114.0 that ran and failed on every page load, and four one-time upgrade steps that were saving English text into the database on non-English sites. Both found on a real server; both now guarded by the test suite.

1.114.0

A price can now be given for the whole lot, not only per unit. Vendors quote both ways — "118.00 for the 25 kg" is not something you should have to divide in your head — so each purchase line now has a small switch under its cost box: per unit or lot. In lot mode you type the total off the invoice and the per-unit price appears beside it.

The same choice is on the item page when you add stock by hand: Price given → per unit / per box / for the whole delivery.

The total you type is the number that gets stored. That matters more than it sounds: 100.00 split over 3 units is 33.3333 each, and three of those is 99.9999. Storing only the unit price would mean reopening the entry to find a total nobody was ever charged. The lot total is kept as typed and the unit price is worked out from it, every time.

Correcting the quantity of a lot-priced entry re-splits the same total — the invoice does not change because the box turned out to hold 26 rather than 25. On a purchase line the lot price is divided by what actually arrived, falling back to what was ordered while the delivery is still outstanding; a returned quantity does not re-rate the goods.

Everything downstream — average cost, recipes, margins, reports — carries on reading one per-unit figure and never needs to know how it was typed. Verified end to end on a real server.

1.113.4

The Produce screen is fixed properly: material name, quantity, unit, cost and the Spoiled box are back on one line. The real cause was a single stray } in the stylesheet. A stray brace makes the browser silently throw away the rule that follows it — no warning, anywhere — and the rule being thrown away was the one that lays those rows out. Before that it had been eating the Spoiled box's styling, which is why that sat on its own line too.

On a phone (under 560px) the name still takes its own line, on purpose. The test suite now measures the row in a real browser at six widths and checks the stylesheet parses at all.

1.113.3

Stopped a warning WordPress wrote to the log on every page load: translations were being set up after the first thing that needed them, rather than before.

1.113.2

Makes the purchases fix in 1.113.1 actually take effect. The installer only re-runs when the database version changes, so correcting it fixed the code without repairing any site. The missing tables are now created on update. Sites that already have them are unaffected.

1.113.1

Fixed: sale locations showed nothing at all on newer MySQL. The query counting what is on each shelf used lines as a column name, which MySQL 8 treats as a reserved word — the whole query failed and every location quietly reported no items, no units and no value. It failed silently, so it looked like empty shelves rather than an error.

Fixed: a brand-new installation had no purchases. The three purchase tables were written out in the installer and never actually created. Existing sites are unaffected — they have had those tables since an older version — but a fresh install gave you no receiving, no vendor bills and no landed cost. That matters for the second company.

Also fixed a warning written to the log on every page load, and added checks so none of these can return: every table the installer describes must actually be created, no column alias may be a reserved word, and nothing may translate before WordPress is ready.

1.113.0

Fixed the mangled material list on the Produce screen. Names were being crushed to a couple of letters per line with the quantity box printed on top of them. The row could not wrap, while the substitutes strip at the end of it demanded the full width — so it took that width from the name. The row wraps properly now: the name is the only part that gives way, the boxes you type into keep their size, and on a phone the name gets a line of its own.

A production run can now carry a note. A field on the Produce screen — batch number, a new supplier's wax, whoever was on the bench. It is saved with the run and shown in the Production report and its CSV.

1.112.3

The real cause: the recipe screen was never telling the server that a line was labour. The save built the right information and then, on the very next line, rebuilt the list without it. So every labour line was filed as an ordinary cost the moment it was saved — which is why it came back in the wrong section, and why it never reached the Labour report.

The two earlier fixes were both real, but neither could help while nothing was being sent. Apologies for the round trips.

If you already have labour sitting under "Други разходи": tap "Това е труд" under the row and save. It will stick now.

1.112.2

A cost line can now be moved between Labour and Other costs in one tap. Under each row there is a small "Това е труд" / "Не е труд" link. Nothing is retyped and no amount changes — only which section the line belongs to.

This is the repair for a line you named yourself. The automatic fix only recognises the words "Labour" and "Труд"; anything of your own — "Изливане", for instance — it deliberately will not guess at. Now it is one tap rather than deleting the line and adding it again.

1.112.1

Fixed: a labour line came back as an ordinary "other cost" when you reopened the recipe — and saving again made that permanent. The recipe screen was sending the editor the label, the amount and the basis, but not the fact that the line was labour. So it drew in the wrong section, and since the editor sends back what it was given, the next save filed it away as overhead. That is also why it never reached the Labour report.

Lines named "Труд" or "Labour" are put back automatically when you update. A line you named yourself — "Изработка", say — needs ticking back into the Labour section by hand, once: the repair only recognises the two standard words and will not guess at the rest.

The Labour tab now also lists what your recipes charge, separately from what production actually cost. Its figures come from production runs, so it stayed empty until you next made something — correct, but indistinguishable from broken. It now shows both: work already booked on runs, and what each recipe will charge next time.

1.112.0

Labour is now its own line on a recipe. The "Other costs" card has split — a Labour section of its own at the top, overhead and misc below it. It is optional: leave it blank and nothing changes. Fill it in and it counts towards the product's cost exactly as before, but the app now knows which part of that cost is work.

Enter it as an amount, or as hours. Set an hourly rate and you can type 0.25 h on a recipe instead of a lev figure. Changing the rate re-prices every recipe that uses hours — never silently: you see exactly which products would move and by how much, and only then an Apply button. Stock you have already made, past production runs and the value on your shelves are not touched.

New Labour tab in Reports (manager only, since it is wages): total labour for the period, hours worked, and labour as a share of production cost. Then every product summed — runs, units made, hours, labour, labour per unit, and what the current recipe would charge for the same work beside it, so a recipe that has drifted is easy to spot. Sortable, with CSV. Reports is now tabbed, and the tab is in the address so a refresh keeps you where you were.

Recipe lines already named "Труд" or "Labour" are marked as labour for you — nothing is deleted and no amount changes. Production runs from before this update show "—" rather than a guessed figure. Also fixed: the Production report priced old runs at today's recipe cost, so a finished run's figure moved whenever a material price did; it now shows what the run actually cost.

1.111.0

Sixteen buttons that did nothing now work. This deployment blocks the browser's own pop-up boxes — they never appear and never complain, the browser simply answers "no" for you. Every button that asked a question that way looked broken. Affected: Issue note, Delete draft, Cancel note, Delete item, Delete order, Remove a sale from an order, Delete purchase, Publish held units to the shop, Pull published units back, Set a partner's price, Add a new unit (item form and recipe), Create an item from an unrecognised barcode, Type a barcode by hand, Reset all translations and Overwrite shop quantities.

A yes/no question is now asked in the button itself: press once and it turns and tells you what is about to happen, press again and it does it. Touch anything else and it stands down. Destructive actions turn red, ordinary confirmations orange. A question that needs a number or a word — how many units, a price, a unit name — opens a small field right where you pressed.

1.110.0

One place now decides what a thing costs. The rule — a hand-typed override, then a subcontractor's rate, then what it actually cost to make, then the recipe, then the purchase history — was written out in four different files. They had drifted apart. Four real differences died with the copies:

  • A product with a labour or overhead line showed a price-including-VAT lower than its own ex-VAT cost (5.70 net / 3.24 incl. on the example recipe). Now 5.70 / 6.24.
  • Switching the costing basis only re-costed recipes — the item page and new till sales kept the old figure.
  • The item form's "calculated" cost echoed the manual override, so you could never see what the recipe charged.

Also fixed: a delivery and a production run on the same day sorted by accident rather than by time, which moved the value of held stock; voiding a production run could leave an unrecoverable half-state; and saving one setting rewrote all of them, so two people editing different settings could undo each other.

Retired the old physical-store feature. It had no screens left, but it still cost an extra database read on every single stock movement and still showed a tick box that did nothing. Sale locations replaced it long ago. No data is deleted. Catalogue and stock-report pages are now noticeably lighter.

1.109.0

Fixes from a full logic, quality and security review. The important ones affect money and production:

VAT is no longer charged when the company is not VAT-registered — purchase and order totals now behave like the till (no VAT, gross equals net), which directly affects a non-VAT company. Recording spoilage on a normal production run no longer wrongly blocks it. Checkout is now one transaction so a mid-way failure cannot leave a half-written sale, and a duplicate item across two cart lines can no longer oversell.

Also: editing a stock movement is now administrator-only; stock cost figures are consistent across the item page, till and recipes; a best-before date can be corrected; archived materials are no longer offered as substitutes; and the self-updater and shop-bridge link are hardened (mandatory https + checksum).

1.108.0

Fixed: the filter buttons would not save. Every row you typed was being discarded - the editor opens in a slide-out panel and the code reading your input was looking in the wrong part of the page, so the labels never registered. Nothing was wrong with what you entered.

Materials can now carry a best-before date. When you receive stock there is an optional Best before box, belonging to that delivery rather than to the material - two batches of the same wax rarely go off on the same day. A Goes off panel then lists the dated deliveries, soonest first, warning when one has passed its date or is within a month of it.

1.107.0

Pin your own filter buttons above the product and material lists. The categories you reach for daily become one tap instead of a dropdown, alongside the existing Low and Archived.

The Buttons control opens an editor: name each one, pick its category, say whether it only shows what is running low, and choose whether it belongs on Products, Materials or both. Pressing the button already applied clears it. The set is shared, so everyone reaches for the same shortcuts.

1.106.0

Every production run now records what it actually cost - materials at that day's prices plus the recipe's labour and overhead, worked out from what really went in, substitutions and spoilage included.

What it has cost to make appears on the item page: every run, its unit cost, and the change since the run before. And a made product is now costed the way a bought one already was - the average of what the stock you are holding actually cost. This moves margins on made goods, for the first time measuring what happened rather than what was planned.

Runs made before this release are left uncosted rather than guessed at, because inventing today's prices for last year's batch would draw a flat line on the very trend this exists to show. Cost them individually if you want them included.

1.105.0

Change the material at the moment of production. Every line on the produce screen can now be swapped for something else and its amount adjusted. It opens on the recipe, because that is what usually happens.

Declare what can stand in for a line, with its own amount. One sheet of A4 or half a sheet of A3 or two of A5 - at production those are one tap and the amount is already worked out. Substitutes you have enough of are shown plainly; ones you are short of are dimmed, so you can see which swaps are actually open to you.

The run consumes exactly what you confirmed and the ledger records what it stood in for. Nothing about costing changes, and anyone who never swaps anything sees the screen they saw before.

1.104.1

Prices under a stotinka are shown properly. Buy wax by the kilo and a gram costs 0.0035, which used to print as 0.00 - making a cheap bulk material look free. Any figure below 1 now shows up to four decimals; anything from 1 upwards is unchanged.

Nothing was ever lost: the columns already stored four decimals and the boxes already accepted them, so your existing prices are correct and will simply read correctly now. No re-entry needed.

1.104.0

Stock value on the item list. A new column shows what is on the shelf for each item - quantity times unit cost, ex-VAT - and it sorts like the others. On a phone it reads as worth X beside the unit cost.

Under the list is a total over whatever you are looking at, so filtering to a category or to materials moves it. Items that cannot honestly be valued are left out rather than counted as zero: a service is never in stock, and an item with no cost recorded is unknown, not free.

1.103.0

Supplier is now a real link. On any item, under Stock & sourcing, pick the partner you buy it from instead of typing a name. The item page links to them and their page lists what you buy from them. The free-text name stays for someone who is not a partner yet, and steps aside once one is linked.

One control, not two. A service used to have a separate Performed by picker hidden in Classification - the same fact, so it is now one field in one place, with only the label changing.

A linked supplier also sets the VAT on what the item costs: buy from someone who is not registered and their price is treated as final, instead of having your own rate added to it.

1.102.0

Administrators can delete sales outright. Open a sale and, at the bottom, Delete sale - two taps, because it cannot be undone. Voiding is unchanged and is still the right tool for a real sale that went wrong: it keeps the receipt, the reason and the trail.

Clearing test data in bulk: on the Sales list, Select turns on a tick per receipt, with select-all. The button names the number before it will act, and only the second press deletes.

Deleting is built on top of voiding: the goods go back to their location and anything the sale put on a supplier's bill is cancelled first, then the paperwork is removed. Every deletion is written to the audit trail, and the whole thing is administrator-only.

1.101.0

Selling a service now credits the subcontracted work inside it. A product gets its bought-in work credited at the production run that makes it - but a service is never produced, so nothing ever walked its recipe and a partner's work sitting inside a service you provide was never credited at all. Selling the service is the moment that work is used, so the recipe is walked then.

It follows nesting, multiplying the quantities through. Selling a stocked product still credits nobody a second time - its run already did - and voiding such a sale cancels everything it accrued.

1.100.1

Say who performs a service, from the item itself. Editing a service now offers Performed by - the partner who does that work for you, or We do this ourselves. Until now the only place that could set it was the Add service drawer on a partner's page, so any service made another way, or made before 1.99.0, credited nobody when it sold.

If selling a service was not showing on the supplier's page, this is why: open the service, pick the partner under Performed by, save. Sales from then on land on their running bill. The item page now says who performs it, and links to them.

1.100.0

Correct what a past sale cost you. Open any sale and a manager now sees a Cost & profit card: what each line was recorded as costing, what the same line would cost today, and a box to put it right. Profit and margin update as you type, so you see the effect before saving.

Use current costs fills every line from today's figures in one click - for sales costed before the VAT fixes in 1.99.1-1.99.3, that is the correction you want. A line marked differs is one whose recorded cost no longer matches what it would cost now.

Every correction is written to the audit trail, and costs stay hidden from anyone below manager.

1.99.3

A cost is no longer grossed up by VAT nobody charged. The VAT on what something COSTS you is charged by whoever sells it to you, so work from a supplier who is not registered now shows their price as final instead of having 20% added to it.

A recipe now grosses component by component. A product made from a registered supplier's material AND an unregistered subcontractor's work used to have the whole total grossed at one rate that applied to neither - so the cost, and every profit figure worked out from it, was wrong.

1.99.2

A supplier who charges no VAT is no longer billed 20% of it. What a subcontractor bills you now follows THEIR registration, taken from the bill itself - not your own status, and not the rate sitting on the item. This affects every service, including ones added before this release.

And a new service is no longer created at 20%: work you only ever buy has no sale VAT to speak of, so it starts at 0. Tick We also sell this at a till and it takes your own rate instead, because what you charge a customer is your business and not the supplier's.

1.99.1

The vendor VAT box now actually moves the lines. Unticking This vendor is VAT registered left every line already on the purchase at its old rate, so the VAT on screen stayed wrong until you saved and reloaded. It now re-rates the whole document the moment you toggle it, both ways.

Starting a purchase from a partner's own page never adopted their VAT status either, so the box came up unticked whoever the vendor was. It now adopts their status and payment terms straight away.

And a company that charges no VAT no longer sees 20% added to the retail column: a genuine 0% rate was being read as missing and quietly replaced with 20.

1.99.0

Subcontracted services. A service can now name the partner who performs it, and using that work credits them automatically - no purchase to remember, no line to type. Create one from the partner's new Services tab: name it, say what you pay them, save.

A service can go in a recipe. It carries its cost into the product, is marked subcontracted, and is never counted, never short and never a reason a run cannot go ahead. You are credited when the work is USED - at the production run, or at the till for a service sold on its own - so the subcontractor is owed in the month they did it.

What you owe lands on one rolling bill per supplier, which is an ordinary purchase underneath, so payments, balance, overdue and the statement all work on it already. Voiding a run or a sale cancels what it accrued, and cannot double-cancel on a retry. Services you already had name no supplier and behave exactly as before.

1.98.1

Add a service straight from the purchase that pays for it. The quick-add drawer on a purchase now has the A service - never in stock tick, so a courier or a subcontractor can be added to the catalogue without leaving the purchase you are entering.

The drawer also stops showing a VAT box when the company is not registered for VAT - it was missed in 1.97.0.

1.98.0

You can now buy a service from a supplier - a courier, subcontracted engraving, a design fee. Mark the item as a service and put it on a purchase like anything else: it carries its price and VAT, counts in full toward what you owe that supplier, and simply never touches stock. Until now such a line would have failed silently, retrying for ever while the screen said nothing.

A service no longer has to be something you sell. The tick means "never in stock" - whether it is a product you sell that way (a workshop) or a material you buy that way (a courier) is the ordinary product/material choice, made separately. Existing services are unaffected.

1.97.0

An installation can now be a company that is not registered for VAT. New switch in Settings: This company is registered for VAT. Turn it off and no VAT is added to any price, so net and gross are one number everywhere.

Receipts and invoices stop showing a VAT line at all - not even a zero. A business that is not registered must not issue a document implying VAT, and "VAT 0.00" is exactly that.

What your suppliers charge you counts in full as your cost. Until now VAT was stripped out of purchase costs as reclaimable input tax. A company that is not registered reclaims nothing, so leaving it in is the honest figure - otherwise every cost was understated and every margin flattered by the VAT rate.

VAT boxes disappear from the item form and the VAT tile from the Sales page, since they would change nothing. The rates stored on your items are kept, so registering later brings every price straight back. Nothing changes for an existing installation: registered is the default.

1.96.0

Log the materials spoiled while making something. Every production run, and every custom order, now has a small spoiled box beside each material: the wax spilled, the jar broken while pouring, the ribbon cut wrong. It comes off stock straight away and is recorded as scrap against that material, so it shows in the material's history and can be reviewed later.

This is separate from the scrap box you already had, which is for finished units that came out defective. One is about what never reached the piece; the other about pieces that were not good enough.

On a custom order the spoiled material is part of what the piece cost - it was made once, so what it really took is knowable. On a repeat product the recipe is left alone (one run's accident cannot be written into a recipe shared by everything ever made), the material still leaves stock as scrap, and the run reports what that waste was worth.

Spoiled material counts toward the shortage warning, so a run cannot pass the check and then drive a material negative. Cancelling a run puts the spoiled material back along with everything else.

1.95.0

Custom orders - one-off pieces made to order. A new Custom order screen, beside Produce: name the piece, add the materials as you use them, set the price, and save. The materials come off the shelf straight away, the piece becomes a product of its own with a true cost, and it is ready to sell.

It tells you whether the price works before you make it. As you add materials you see the cost of the whole job, the cost of each piece, and the margin against the price you are quoting - in red if you are about to sell under cost. If you have used more of something than you actually have, it says so, by name, before you save.

Enter what the whole job used, not fractions per piece: 4 kg of wax and 40 wicks for 40 candles, and each candle is costed at a tenth of a kilo without you doing the division.

Then choose where it goes - push it to a stall and sell it at the till, or put it on an order for a named customer. There is an Archive button for when it has gone, so commissions do not clutter the catalogue. Nothing is archived automatically.

Made in a single step, so a dropped connection can never leave a half-made product behind: if anything fails, nothing is created at all.

1.94.0

Profit and margin on the Sales page. Alongside the takings you now get what those sales actually earned: Profit (revenue less what the goods cost you) and Margin as a percentage of it. Every receipt in the list carries its own profit and margin too, so a bad day - or a product being sold under cost - is visible at a glance rather than buried in a total.

Profit is measured honestly. It uses revenue excluding VAT (that money was never yours) and after refunds (goods that came back were neither sold nor cost you anything). A loss shows as a negative figure in red, not as a small profit.

Each sale now remembers what its goods cost at the time it was rung up. Without that, changing a material price would silently restate the profit on every sale you ever made. Sales from before this update fall back to the product's current cost, so older figures are an estimate - anything sold from now on is exact.

Cost is manager-level information, so profit and margin are left out of the page - and out of the CSV export - for anyone below that, rather than merely hidden.

1.93.3

Fix: on iPhone the till zoomed in and stayed zoomed. Tapping the search box, the barcode field or a discount made iOS magnify the whole page - pushing the scan button and half the product grid off the right of the screen - and it never zoomed back out. iOS does this to any text field smaller than 16px; every field in the app is now 16px on touch devices, so there is nothing left to trigger it. Pinch-zoom still works normally if a seller wants it.

Desktop is untouched: the rule applies only to touch screens, so the back office looks exactly as before.

1.93.2

The product photo now fills the whole width of its tile. It was leaving the picture short of the box and holding the box at a fixed height on phones, so the photos looked stranded rather than filling the tile.

The height now follows the tile's own width, so photos grow and shrink with the screen instead of sitting at one size. Whatever shape you uploaded - tall, wide or square - is cropped to fill rather than letterboxed.

Always two products per row on a phone. On narrower handsets the grid was dropping to a single product per row with an enormous picture; it is now two everywhere from the smallest phone up.

1.93.1

Bigger product photos on the till. The picture was squeezed into a 62px strip so the name could take as many rows as it liked - on a stall, the photo is how a seller finds a product, so it now fills most of the tile and scales with the column width.

Product names are capped at two rows, with the rest trimmed to an ellipsis. A long name no longer stretches its tile and shrinks its own photo, so every tile in a row is the same shape and the prices line up. Hovering a tile still shows the full name.

1.93.0

Every sale location is now its own installable app. A seller adds their stall's till to their phone's home screen and taps straight into it - no app, no menu, no picking a location first. Each one installs separately, with the stall's name under it and its own coloured icon carrying the stall's initials, so three tills on one phone are told apart at a glance.

A till app is locked to its stall. It can only sell from the location it was installed for, so a sale can never be rung up against the wrong stall and stock always comes off the right shelf. Managers still switch freely from the main app.

Handing one to a seller: open the location, press Till app, and show them the QR code - they scan it, open the link, and use their browser's "Add to Home Screen". The link is there to send by message too.

Signing in no longer loses the till: opening a till and logging in used to drop you into the back office, and now lands you on the till you were opening. An installed till also works offline as itself, rather than falling back to the back-office screen - the last place a seller at a market should end up.

1.92.3

Fix: adding a service to a sale location did nothing. The table holding each location's service menu was never actually created on existing installs - it was created only by a repair routine that had already run once and never runs again - so every save failed while the screen cheerfully said it had worked. Installing this version creates the table; add your services again and they will stick. Saving now reports a real failure instead of a false success.
